best-broadway-shows-2020.intro:
Looking back at Broadway shows that opened in 2020, we find a snapshot of a theatrical season cut dramatically short by the pandemic, yet one that still delivered several memorable productions in the brief window before theaters went dark in March of that year.

**A Soldier's Play** stands as the highest-rated show from this truncated season, bringing Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama to Broadway for the first time. The production's exploration of racial tensions within a segregated World War II Army unit resonates with critics who praise both its historical significance and contemporary relevance. Kenny Leon's direction earns particular acclaim for drawing out the play's layered examination of identity and injustice.

Ivo van Hove's **West Side Story** revival represents the season's most polarizing production. The Belgian director's deconstructed approach—incorporating video projections and abandoning Jerome Robbins' iconic choreography—splits critical opinion sharply. While some reviewers celebrate the fresh perspective on the classic musical, others find the conceptual choices distract from the timeless Bernstein-Sondheim score.

On the comedic front, **Grand Horizons** offers Bess Wohl's wry take on long-term marriage and late-life reinvention. Critics respond warmly to the play's sharp dialogue and the chemistry of its veteran cast, though some note the material occasionally treads familiar ground.

The top-rated shows from early 2020 average a solid 74/100 critic score, reflecting a season that, while brief, showcased Broadway's range from serious drama to experimental revivals to character-driven comedy. The year isn't without its disappointments, as "Beaches, A New Musical" struggles to rise above sentimental material despite strong performances, reminding audiences that beloved films don't always translate successfully to the stage. Overall, the season's average critical score of 72 out of 100 reflects a healthy mix of ambitious successes and noble failures. best-broadway-plays-2020.intro:
Looking back at Broadway's 2020 season from our vantage point in May 2026, we see a year that was tragically cut short by the pandemic, yet still managed to deliver several memorable productions before theaters went dark in March. The shows that opened during those brief winter months continue to resonate, offering a poignant snapshot of Broadway at a pivotal moment.

**A Soldier's Play** stands as the highest-rated production from this period, bringing Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama to Broadway for the first time. Critics consistently praise the production's powerful performances and the play's enduring examination of racism within the military, proving that great writing transcends its era. The show earns a 79/100 average across reviews, reflecting widespread critical acclaim.

Ivo van Hove's controversial reimagining of **West Side Story** generates notably divided responses, with its video-heavy staging and departure from Jerome Robbins' iconic choreography sparking heated debate among critics. While some embrace the bold reinterpretation, others find it at odds with the material's essential nature—a split that makes it one of the season's most discussed productions.

Rounding out the top-rated plays, **Grand Horizons** offers lighter fare with Bess Wohl's comedy about late-life divorce, earning praise particularly for its ensemble cast. Meanwhile, **My Name is Lucy Barton** showcases Laura Linney in a performance that critics universally celebrate, even when they're less convinced by the adaptation itself.

With an average critic score of 74/100, these productions represent a solid if abbreviated season. Browse the complete rankings below to discover which 2020 productions best match your theatrical interests.

best-broadway-plays-2021.intro:
As we reach May 2026, the Broadway productions that opened in 2021 continue to demonstrate the remarkable resilience and creativity that defined the theater industry's post-pandemic return. That season marked a pivotal moment when stages reopened and artists delivered some of the most innovative and talked-about work in recent memory.

Leading the critical rankings is "Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club," an immersive revival that transforms the August Wilson Theatre into the decadent world of Weimar Germany. Critics consistently praise its bold reimagining of the classic musical, with the environmental staging creating an unforgettable theatrical experience. Close behind is "The Lehman Trilogy," Sam Mendes' epic examination of American capitalism told through the rise and fall of the Lehman Brothers financial dynasty. The production's ability to condense 164 years of history into a riveting evening of theater, powered by just three actors, earns widespread acclaim.

The 2021 season also brought experimental works like "Dana H.," which pushes theatrical boundaries with its unconventional approach to storytelling, and "Is This a Room," a verbatim drama drawn from FBI transcripts that proves documentary theater can be as gripping as any fiction. Meanwhile, Marianne Elliott's gender-swapped "Company" offers a fresh perspective on Stephen Sondheim's classic, while plays like "Pass Over," "Clyde's," and "Slave Play" tackle urgent contemporary themes with intelligence and craft.

These productions collectively achieve an impressive 82 out of 100 average critic score, reflecting a season that balanced artistic ambition with theatrical excellence. Whether you're drawn to immersive spectacle, intimate drama, or bold social commentary, exploring the highest-rated shows from this landmark season offers a comprehensive view of Broadway at its most vital.

The year's theatrical landscape proves particularly notable for its diversity of voices and forms. Jordan E. Cooper's audacious satire **Ain't No Mo'** tackles Black American life with wild, uproarious energy, while Tom Stoppard's deeply personal **Leopoldstadt** explores Holocaust history with emotional power and epic scope. best-broadway-plays-2023.intro:

Contemporary voices also flourish among the top-rated shows, from Branden Jacobs-Jenkins's Pulitzer-winning "Fat Ham" to Branden Jacobs-Jenkins's searing family drama "Appropriate," both demonstrating that new American playwriting remains vital and uncompromising.
